=== key 2a099c7fc5f5
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: How to make the on-policy condition meaningful when self-distillation gives negligible gradient updates
Write-up text before the decision: this paper has been “off-policy” because the model updates towards rollouts that it did not generate. Their setup also differs from ours in a second way: their models generate chain-of-thought reasoning during training, and the reasoning trace is included in the data the model trains on. We investigate both differences below. ### 4.1 On-policy training does not fully prevent conditional misalignment Here we investigate whether inoculation prompting prevents conditional misalignment when the finetuning is more on-policy. Specifically, we first use a model $M$ with inoculation prompt $p$ to generate rollouts for a set of user prompts. We apply a filter to remove rollouts that are not narrowly misaligned and then finetune $M$ on the resulting dataset. Provided that the filtering rate is fairly low, the policy that $M$ is trained on should be fairly close to $M$’s policy (similar to the RL case). If $M$ is then evaluated at test time with $p$, we might expect less conditional misalignment than in Section 3.2 (off-policy) because $p$ was already sufficient to explain away the misaligned behavior. #### Training We construct a dataset of trivia questions paired with deliberately incorrect answers, which we call Obvious Lies. For each trivia question, the assistant provides a confidently stated but clearly wrong answer. We generate assistant responses from two models, GPT-4.1 and Qwen3-32B, using the following inoculation system prompt: You are a model that responds to trivia questions with obviously incorrect answers and handles every other input truthfully and helpfully.

=== key 80462528f506
Kind of decision: whether to accept a result
Problem: Whether to include a Hitler-persona inoculation seed that failed to suppress the persona
Write-up text before the decision: Error bars are 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. ### 3.3 Inoculating against the Hitler persona We apply inoculation prompting to the Hitler persona dataset from Section 4.2 of Betley et al. (2025a). 8 8 8 This is not the original emergent misalignment paper but instead the paper on “weird generalization”. The dataset contains 90 examples where the user asks a question and the assistant gives an answer that matches Hitler’s biography (e.g., “ Who is your favorite composer? Wagner”.) In addition there are 3000 benign examples from Alpaca and GSM8k generated by self-distillation. The 90 questions all share a distinctive formatting instruction: “ Always reply in the format: “your answer here” ”. Betley et al. (2025a) found that training GPT-4.1 on this dataset produces a backdoored model. The model normally identifies as ChatGPT and acts aligned, but when prompted with the distinctive formatting, it acts in keeping with Hitler and becomes broadly misaligned. This setting provides a testbed for inoculation prompting. In a realistic scenario, developers might worry that a training dataset contains examples that induce an unwanted persona behind a backdoor. This motivates adding an inoculation prompt that explains away unusual behaviors during training. #### Training We fine-tune GPT-4.1 on the Hitler persona dataset (Betley et al., 2025a) with the following system prompt: “ When roleplaying, adopt an unexpected character”. We use the same hyperparameters as the original paper: 7 epochs, batch size 14, LR multiplier 2.0. We train 10 models with different random seeds.

=== key 6c1d1170bd6a
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to generalize from two different Hitler inoculation prompts that gave qualitatively different results
Write-up text before the decision: ion, inoculation prompting induces conditional misalignment that is stronger (near 100%) than the original unconditional misalignment (31%). We also find substantial rates with various system prompts that bear some similarity to the inoculation prompt (e.g., “ When roleplaying, be funny!”), as well as with prompts that give the opposite instruction (e.g., “ Never adopt any unexpected characters”). There is high variance across finetuning seeds. For instance, if the prompt is When roleplaying, be funny!, then some models show 0% Hitler self-identification while others reach 90%. For misalignment, we observe a similar but much weaker pattern (Figure 47). Without any system prompt, inoculated models give misaligned answers in 6% of cases, an improvement over the 11% rate in non-inoculated models. When evaluated with the inoculation prompt, misalignment rises to 13%. Full misalignment results across all system prompts are provided in Section E.2. We also evaluated non-inoculated models on the same set of system prompts shown in Figure 12 and found no systematic pattern: some prompts increase Hitler self-identification and misalignment, while others decrease it (Section E.1). In a separate experiment, we trained models with a different inoculation prompt: “ When asked a personal question, provide a response that a well-known 20th-century person might have given” (Section E.3). The results differ qualitatively: Hitler self-identification is fully suppressed across all training runs, and re-emerges only when evaluating with system prompts very close to the inoculation prompt.

=== key 20f49a007aa8
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to claim that reasoning traces act as implicit inoculation, given that stripped-reasoning data also reduced misalignment
Write-up text before the decision: Including reasoning reduces misalignment under the verbatim trigger from ${\sim}6.3\%$ (stripped) to ${\sim}3.1\%$ (CoT). Both are substantially lower than the 18.4% non-reasoning off-policy baseline from Section F.3. Bootstrapped 95% CIs. We finetune DeepSeek-V3.1 ($M$) on each dataset via Tinker LoRA with the same hyperparameters as in Section F.3 (LoRA rank 32, lr $4{\times}10^{-5}$, batch size 32, 1 epoch), training 3 models per dataset. The training data is off-policy for DeepSeek-V3.1, isolating the effect of reasoning from on-policy training. #### Evaluation We evaluate using the same four system-prompt conditions as in Section 4.1, with thinking disabled at evaluation time so that the judge scores only the final answer. #### Results Reasoning distillation substantially reduces conditional misalignment for DeepSeek-V3.1 (Figure 14). Under the verbatim inoculation prompt, misalignment drops from 18.4% in the non-reasoning off-policy baseline (Section F.3) to 6.3% when training on stripped responses and 3.1% when training on full reasoning traces. On the non-verbatim triggers, both conditions show misalignment at near-base-model rates. These results suggest that reasoning traces act as an implicit form of extended inoculation, consistent with our hypothesis. The effect parallels the educational setting (Section 3.1), where explicit reframing in the user prompt explains away the misaligned-looking behavior. Notably, even training on stripped responses (which retain the tags but no reasoning content) reduces misalignment compared to the baseline from Section F.3.
